prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- South African Giniel De Villiers is the new leader of the Dakar Rally after he won Thursday's 12th special stage and Spaniard Carlos Sainz was forced to pull out following a dramatic crash. The stricken Volkswagen of Carlos Sainz after he careered down a ravine on stage 12 of the Dakar Rally. De Villiers, who was claiming his third stage triumph, brought his Volkswagen across the line in four hours, six minutes and 43 seconds -- over 16 minutes  ahead of team-mate Mark Miller, who lies second overall. American Robert Gordon (Hummer) was third on the stage, the same as his overall position. The route from Fiambala to La Rioja was reduced by 30 kilometers, leaving the special stage at 223km, as organizers accepted the Argentinian authorities' request to shorten it because of the archaeological discoveries made a month ago in the Fiambala region of Catamarca province. Two-time world rally champion Sainz, who was leading after six stage victories, had his dream of winning his first Dakar ended when, 79km into the stage, his Volkswagen crashed into a dry riverbed. His co-driver, Frenchman Michel Perin, suffered a shoulder injury and both had to be evacuated by helicopter for medical attention. Perin told PA Sport: "We had made a small mistake in the first part. We took the wrong direction at a Y crossing but it was not too bad because we did end up on the right trail. We were tailing Giniel De Villiers, who had started about 10 minutes after us, so it was still sort of okay. There was a hidden way-point indicated as 'danger' -- but it should have been indicated as 'extremely dangerous'. "The car behind us, Nani Roma's car, would have fallen in the same hole as we did if we had not been there already. I'm okay, I just have something broken in my arm, but I'm all right." De Villiers said: "It was really a tough stage. In places we would go around in circles for 15 minutes to find the right trail. It was very dangerous and the sand was really soft. "We stopped one time to deflate our tyres, then a second time in a huge canyon with tons of boulders. My co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz had to get out of the car to find a way out. It was really a tough day." Miller added: "I can tell you that this was a very demanding stage. I cannot even imagine how the amateurs will make it to the finish today. It was not just difficult, navigation was almost impossible. "It was a long series of horror situations from start to finish. "These were the longest 200km in my life. The sun and the sand were so bright that I could not see anything." He added: "It's not good news to know that Carlos had to withdraw. He has an important place in the team." In the motorcycle class, title holder Cyril Despres (KTM) kept his hopes of winning his third crown alive after taking his third stage in a time of 3:57:37 to climb into second spot in the overall standings. However, Despres' Spanish team-mate Marc Coma did not make things easy for the Frenchman as he crossed the line 1:23 behind, to remain out in front with a 1:29:48 advantage. The 12th stage has been the most difficult since the rally began on January 3 in Buenos Aires, with competitiors struggling through sand dunes and rain in western Argentina. Sainz had held a commanding lead in the overall standings at the start of the day, having won six of 10 previous stages.

outputs.L1:
(CNN) -- South African Giniel De Villiers is the new leader of the Dakar Rally after winning Thursday’s 12th special stage, while Spaniard Carlos Sainz was forced to withdraw following a dramatic crash.

The stricken Volkswagen of Carlos Sainz after it careered down a ravine during Stage 12 of the Dakar Rally.

De Villiers, claiming his third stage victory, brought his Volkswagen across the line in four hours, six minutes and 43 seconds—more than 16 minutes ahead of teammate Mark Miller, who sits second overall.

American Robert Gordon, driving a Hummer, finished third on the stage, matching his position in the overall standings.

The route from Fiambala to La Rioja was shortened by 30 kilometers, leaving the special stage at 223 kilometers, after organizers agreed to a request from Argentinian authorities. The change was made because of archaeological discoveries in the Fiambala region of Catamarca province a month earlier.

Two-time world rally champion Sainz, who had been leading after six stage victories, saw his dream of winning his first Dakar come to an end when his Volkswagen crashed into a dry riverbed 79 kilometers into the stage.

His co-driver, Frenchman Michel Perin, suffered a shoulder injury, and both men were evacuated by helicopter for medical attention.

Perin told PA Sport: “We had made a small mistake in the first part. We took the wrong direction at a Y crossing, but it was not too bad because we did end up on the right trail.

“We were tailing Giniel De Villiers, who had started about 10 minutes after us, so it was still sort of okay. There was a hidden waypoint indicated as ‘danger’—but it should have been indicated as ‘extremely dangerous.’

“The car behind us, Nani Roma’s car, would have fallen in the same hole as we did if we had not been there already. I’m okay. I just have something broken in my arm, but I’m all right.”

De Villiers said: “It was really a tough stage. In places, we would go around in circles for 15 minutes to find the right trail. It was very dangerous, and the sand was really soft.

“We stopped once to deflate our tires, then a second time in a huge canyon with tons of boulders. My co-driver, Dirk von Zitzewitz, had to get out of the car to find a way out. It was really a tough day.”

Miller added: “I can tell you that this was a very demanding stage. I cannot even imagine how the amateurs will make it to the finish today. It was not just difficult; navigation was almost impossible.

“It was a long series of horror situations from start to finish.

“These were the longest 200 kilometers of my life. The sun and the sand were so bright that I could not see anything.”

He added: “It’s not good news to know that Carlos had to withdraw. He has an important place in the team.”

In the motorcycle class, defending champion Cyril Despres of KTM kept alive his hopes of winning a third crown by claiming his third stage victory in a time of 3:57:37, moving into second place in the overall standings.

However, Despres’ Spanish teammate Marc Coma did not make things easy for the Frenchman, crossing the line 1:23 behind to retain the overall lead with an advantage of 1:29:48.

The 12th stage was the most difficult since the rally began in Buenos Aires on January 3, with competitors battling sand dunes and rain in western Argentina.

Sainz had held a commanding lead in the overall standings at the start of the day, having won six of the previous 10 stages.

Perin told PA Sport that they had made a minor navigational error early in the stage, choosing the wrong branch at a Y-shaped junction. However, they eventually returned to the correct track and were following De Villiers, who had started roughly 10 minutes later, so the situation still appeared manageable.

According to Perin, a concealed waypoint had been labeled merely as dangerous when it should have carried an extreme-danger warning. He said Nani Roma’s car, which was behind them, would probably have fallen into the same hole had Sainz’s Volkswagen not already been there. Perin added that although he had broken something in his arm, he otherwise felt all right.

De Villiers described the stage as exceptionally challenging. At some points, he said, they spent about 15 minutes driving in circles while searching for the correct route. Conditions were hazardous, with very soft sand.

He said they stopped first to lower the pressure in their tires and later became trapped in a huge canyon filled with large rocks. His co-driver, Dirk von Zitzewitz, had to leave the vehicle to identify an escape route. De Villiers characterized the entire day as extremely difficult.

Miller agreed that the stage had been highly demanding and said he could not imagine how amateur competitors would manage to reach the finish. Beyond the physical difficulty, he said, navigation was nearly impossible.

He described the course as an uninterrupted sequence of frightening situations and called it the longest 200km he had ever experienced. The intense brightness of the sun reflecting from the sand made it almost impossible for him to see.

Miller also said Sainz’s withdrawal was bad news because the Spaniard held an important role within the Volkswagen team.

In the motorcycle category, defending champion Cyril Despres of France kept alive his chances of claiming a third Dakar title. The KTM rider secured his third stage victory in 3:57:37 and rose to second overall.

However, his Spanish KTM teammate Marc Coma remained firmly in control. Coma finished only one minute and 23 seconds behind Despres and retained the overall lead by one hour, 29 minutes and 48 seconds.

Stage 12 was considered the hardest since the rally started in Buenos Aires on January 3, as competitors battled rain and sand dunes in western Argentina.

Sainz had entered the day with a substantial advantage in the overall rankings, having won six of the previous 10 stages.

**LA RIOJA, Argentina (CNN) —** South Africa’s Giniel De Villiers moved into the overall lead of the Dakar Rally after Volkswagen teammate Carlos Sainz crashed out during Thursday’s 12th stage.

Sainz, the rally leader entering the route from Fiambalá to La Rioja, saw his hopes of a first Dakar title end when his Volkswagen Touareg plunged into a ravine early in the timed section.

The two-time world rally champion was unhurt, but co-driver Michel Périn suffered a shoulder injury and was evacuated by helicopter. The accident forced the Spanish-French crew to withdraw.

De Villiers completed the demanding stage without major trouble and assumed first place in the overall standings, 2 minutes, 35 seconds ahead of American teammate Mark Miller.

Sainz had held a commanding advantage of more than 27 minutes over De Villiers before the crash. His retirement dramatically reshaped the race and left Volkswagen’s remaining drivers in control at the front.

De Villiers, seeking his first Dakar crown, must now protect a narrow lead through the closing stages to Buenos Aires. American Robby Gordon remained in contention for a podium finish but trailed the two Volkswagen drivers by a substantial margin.

The Dakar Rally was being held in South America for the first time after security concerns forced organizers to cancel the previous year’s event in Africa.

## Sainz’s Dakar hopes end in ravine as De Villiers wins punishing 12th stage

**LA RIOJA, Argentina —** Carlos Sainz’s commanding bid to win the Dakar Rally ended abruptly when his Volkswagen plunged into a ravine during the 12th stage, injuring co-driver Michel Périn and handing teammate Giniel de Villiers a dramatic stage victory and control of the race.

Sainz, the rally leader and winner of six stages, crashed early in the timed section between Fiambalá and La Rioja after missing a difficult change of direction. His Volkswagen Race Touareg left the route and fell several metres into a rocky gully, coming to rest in a position from which it could not continue.

The former two-time world rally champion escaped without serious injury, but Périn hurt his shoulder in the impact. Medical personnel reached the crew, and the French navigator was evacuated for treatment. Initial reports described the injury as a fractured shoulder blade, although it was not considered life-threatening.

With the car stranded and Périn requiring medical attention, Sainz was forced to retire. The accident erased a lead of more than 27 minutes and brought a sudden end to what had been the strongest campaign of the rally.

“It was a very difficult place,” Sainz said in explaining the accident. The Spaniard indicated that the crew had missed a turn described in the road book and had been unable to avoid the drop once the car left the track.

### De Villiers takes advantage

De Villiers, driving another factory Volkswagen with German co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz, completed the stage fastest. The South African’s victory transformed the overall classification, moving him into the lead ahead of American teammate Mark Miller.

The result also underlined Volkswagen’s continued control of the car category despite the loss of its most successful driver of the event. Before the crash, Sainz had appeared well placed to deliver his first Dakar victory. Instead, de Villiers and Miller were left to contest the final stages at the head of the field.

De Villiers said the day had been exceptionally demanding and that simply finding the correct route had been as important as outright speed. He and von Zitzewitz avoided the costly navigational mistakes that affected much of the field and maintained a controlled pace through the rougher sections.

The South African also encountered the scene of Sainz’s accident and immediately understood that the rally had changed. Although Sainz and Périn were out of the car and receiving assistance, the damaged Volkswagen could not be recovered in time to continue competitively.

### Navigation causes widespread confusion

The crash came during one of the most confusing stages of the rally, with competitors reporting that the road book was difficult to interpret and that tracks were often faint or nonexistent. The route crossed open desert, scrub and broken terrain where numerous parallel paths made it easy to select the wrong direction.

Drivers said small errors quickly became expensive because there were few visual references. Once one competitor took an incorrect line, others often followed the wheel tracks, creating false routes across the landscape.

Several crews spent significant periods searching for hidden waypoints or retracing their path to the last reliable road-book instruction. Competitors described the stage as a day on which concentration and trust between driver and navigator were crucial.

Miller was among those who acknowledged the severity of the navigation challenge. He said crews had to remain cautious because pushing at maximum speed while uncertain of the route carried a high risk of an accident or a major time loss.

Motorcycle competitors voiced similar concerns. Riders reported becoming disoriented in areas where the written directions, compass headings and visible tracks did not appear to correspond clearly. Groups formed as competitors searched together for the correct passage, while others lost substantial time after following misleading tracks.

The complaints reflected a recurring feature of the South American Dakar: unlike conventional rallying, where crews follow a clearly defined road, Dakar competitors must interpret a road book while racing through open terrain. In the Fiambalá region, soft sand, dunes, dry riverbeds and scrub made that task especially hazardous.

### A decisive moment in the rally

Sainz’s retirement represented one of the biggest reversals of the event. He had combined stage-winning speed with relative consistency and had built a margin that appeared sufficient to protect him during the final run toward Buenos Aires.

But the Dakar’s margin for error remained unforgiving. One missed instruction was enough to eliminate the leader and injure one of the sport’s most experienced navigators.

For de Villiers, the victory offered both an opportunity and a warning. He inherited first place, but the circumstances of Sainz’s exit demonstrated that the remaining stages could still overturn the standings.

Volkswagen retained a powerful position with de Villiers and Miller at the front, yet the team’s emphasis shifted immediately from chasing stage wins to bringing its surviving cars safely to the finish. After a day dominated by difficult navigation and Sainz’s spectacular crash, the rally had acquired a new leader—and a reminder that no advantage was secure until Buenos Aires.

**De Villiers takes Dakar lead as Sainz loses time**

SAN RAFAEL, Argentina (Reuters) — South African Giniel de Villiers won the fifth stage of the Dakar Rally to take the overall lead from Volkswagen teammate Carlos Sainz after a difficult run from Neuquen to San Rafael.

De Villiers and German co-driver Dirk von Zitzewitz completed the timed section in 5 hours, 47 minutes, 43 seconds. Volkswagen’s Dieter Depping was second, 2:18 behind, while American Mark Miller finished third at 4:12.

Sainz, who had led the rally after the previous stage, lost time with a puncture and surrendered first place. His French navigator, Michel Perin, said the delay had forced the crew to balance speed against the risk of further trouble.

“We had a puncture and lost several minutes,” Perin said. “After that, we had to be careful because the stage was very long and difficult.”

De Villiers said the route, which included fast tracks, rough ground and dunes, had offered little margin for error.

“It was a very difficult stage,” De Villiers said. “We tried to keep a good rhythm and not make mistakes. To win the stage and take the lead is a very good result, but there is still a long way to go.”

After five stages, De Villiers led Sainz by 2:18 in the overall standings. Miller moved into third place, 6:42 off the lead, giving Volkswagen the top three positions.

Miller said his third-place stage finish reflected a cautious approach on a day when punctures and navigation errors could quickly erase time.

“It was a long day, but a good day for us,” Miller said. “The important thing was to stay out of trouble and bring the car home. We are in a strong position overall.”

The result tightened the battle among the Volkswagen crews, with De Villiers holding only a slim advantage over Sainz and Miller still within striking distance.
